name: Brilacidin
route: Studied as an IV dose, a mouth rinse and a colon-release tablet
status: Not FDA-approved. Most advanced trials are small phase 2 studies; no phase 3 trial is registered
mechanism: A small synthetic molecule that mimics defensins, natural infection-fighting proteins, to disrupt microbes and calm inflammation

article.summary: Brilacidin is an experimental synthetic mimic of the body's defensin proteins, studied for skin infections, radiation mouth sores and bowel inflammation. Human data are small and it is not approved.
article.takeaway: Brilacidin is not a true peptide but a small synthetic molecule designed to behave like defensins, natural proteins that help the body fight microbes.[^1] It began as a possible single-dose antibiotic for skin infections, then was tested as a mouth rinse to prevent severe mouth sores during head and neck cancer radiation and as a treatment for ulcerative proctitis. Human data are limited to small phase 2 studies. In the mouth rinse trial, severe mucositis occurred in 9 of 21 treated patients versus 15 of 25 on placebo.[^2] No phase 3 trial is registered, and brilacidin is not approved for any use.
glance: Investigational; not approved by the FDA
Skin infections, radiation-induced mouth sores, ulcerative proctitis
Intravenous dose, mouth rinse or colon-release tablet (in trials)
Two phase 2 trials with registry records; little peer-reviewed human data

blocks.text: Defensins are small proteins the body makes to fight microbes and to help regulate inflammation. Brilacidin is a small synthetic molecule built to imitate the shape and charge pattern of a defensin, which is why it is called a non-peptide mimetic even though it is grouped with peptide drugs.[^1] Like defensins, it is thought to disrupt microbial membranes and to calm inflammatory signaling.
In laboratory studies it has also shown antifungal and antiviral activity in cells.[^1][^3] Those findings are not evidence of benefit in people.

The sponsor first developed brilacidin as a possible single-dose intravenous antibiotic for serious skin infections.[^4] It has since been tested as a mouth rinse for painful mouth sores (oral mucositis) caused by radiation for head and neck cancer, and in an open-label study of ulcerative proctitis and proctosigmoiditis, two forms of bowel inflammation.[^5] A tablet designed to release in the colon was studied in healthy volunteers. The most advanced studies are phase 2, and no phase 3 trial is listed on ClinicalTrials.gov.

rows: Completed; no results are posted in the registry[^4]
61 adults with head and neck cancer
Severe mucositis in 9 of 21 on brilacidin vs 15 of 25 on placebo (those given at least 55 Gy)[^2]

blocks.text: The mouth rinse figures come from the trial registry, and the study was small. A PubMed search finds no peer-reviewed report of these trials' results as of October 2026, and no larger trial has confirmed them.

items: **Mouth rinse trial:** fatigue (21 vs 13 people), altered taste (17 vs 13) and dry mouth (16 vs 9) were more frequent on brilacidin than on placebo.[^2]
**Serious adverse events** were reported in 8 of 29 people on brilacidin and 5 of 30 on placebo.[^2]
**Unknown:** safety at antibiotic doses, long-term effects and drug interactions are not well documented in published trials.

blocks.text: No confirmatory trial is registered, so brilacidin's future depends on funding and on whether the sponsor starts a phase 3 study. Until a larger controlled trial reports, its benefit in any condition remains unproven.

evidence.label: Early: small phase 2 trials, little published data
evidence.text: Human data come from phase 2 trials of 61 and 215 adults, and only the mouth rinse trial has posted results.[^2][^4] Most other findings are from cells and animals, and none of this supports use outside a trial.

faq.a: No. It is a small synthetic molecule designed to imitate defensins, which are natural proteins, so it is described as a defensin mimetic rather than a peptide.[^1]
No. It is investigational and not approved for any condition. Any online product sold as brilacidin would be unapproved, with unverified contents.

faq.q: Why is a mouth rinse being studied?
faq.a: Radiation to the head and neck often causes painful mouth sores. A rinse lets a drug act on the lining directly, and a small phase 2 trial found fewer severe cases on brilacidin, though it has not been repeated.[^2]
